result: The authors developed a sophisticated fTIR-based optical method (FlyWalker) for tracking insect footfalls with high temporal and spatial resolution, scaled appropriately for Drosophila's small size and rapid walking speed.
status_reasoning: Reviewers explicitly praised the technology as 'very sophisticated,' 'powerful and impressive,' and 'a nice technical innovation.' They requested recognition of similar systems (CatWalk) for rodents with emphasis on scaling to fly size, which the manuscript addresses in C19-C20. No concerns were raised about the technical validity of the method.

result: Flies do not abruptly switch gaits but use a continuum of gait patterns correlated with speed, with tripod gait predominating at all speeds but decreasing in frequency at slower speeds where tetrapod and noncanonical combinations increase.
status_reasoning: Reviewers stated 'there are not discrete transitions in gait, however: the typical tripod gait occurs at all speeds, but with diminishing frequency in slower flies.' They found the data showing differences between fast and slow animals 'fairly convincing,' indicating acceptance of the gradual gait transition findings.

result: Several readouts suggest flies may use distinct neural programs at slow, medium, and fast walking speeds, with abrupt differences in parameters like footprint alignment occurring at speeds (~20 mm/s) that are underrepresented in the dataset.
status_reasoning: Reviewers raised significant concerns about the rationale for dividing animals into three speed groups, asking 'why not 2 groups: above and below average; or 4 groups?' They noted that 'the way they group animals is going to affect their statistical analysis' and requested either statistical verification of the break at 20 mm/s or more animals at low speed to clarify the distribution. This indicates uncertainty about whether distinct neural programs exist.

result: Wild-type fly speeds range from 7.2 to 44.7 mm/s with 28 mm/s most represented, speeds around 20 mm/s are underrepresented, and the distribution shows non-Gaussian outliers in the tails despite fitting a normal distribution by Shapiro-Wilk test.
status_reasoning: Reviewers questioned how outliers were determined and on what basis they were excluded, stating 'How were outliers determined and on what basis were they then excluded?' They also asked whether a statistical test could verify the split at 20 mm/s or if more animals at low speed could be measured. This indicates uncertainty about the characterization of the speed distribution.

result: Multiple gait parameters vary systematically with speed in wild-type flies, including stance/swing phase durations, step period, step length, swing speed, stance linearity, footprint clustering, footprint alignment, and contralateral leg phase variability.
status_reasoning: While reviewers acknowledged the data is 'extensive' and provides 'a rich database for future workers,' they expressed 'significant concerns about some of the data analysis,' specifically that 'these statistical methods were not adequate' and recommended ANOVA or equivalent non-parametric tests followed by appropriate post-hoc tests instead of the t-tests and Mann-Whitney U-tests used. This statistical concern affects confidence in all speed-dependent parameter comparisons.

result: Sensory-deprived flies (nan36a and 5-40Leg>TNT genotypes) walked slower with deficient step precision (increased step length, jitter, and footprint variability) especially at slow speeds, but maintained tripod gait and interleg coordination.
status_reasoning: Reviewers described this as 'a surprising result' and 'the most interesting aspect of the work,' explicitly stating that 'sensory deficient flies walked slower than wild-type flies, but maintained a typical tripod gait with normal left–right and interlimb coordination' while 'stance traces showed some defects.' They found this surprising because it contrasts with stick insects, indicating they accepted the findings as valid.

result: Trends in sensory-deprived flies resemble those in faster wild-type flies, and defects are more pronounced at slow speeds, suggesting flies walking at fast speeds are less dependent on sensory feedback and use a largely CPG-based system.
status_reasoning: Reviewers explicitly stated 'the walking of sensory-deprived flies suggests that flies may be less dependent on sensory feedback when they walk fast because defects were more pronounced in slow flies,' indicating acceptance of this interpretation. They contrasted this with stick insects that 'walk very slowly and rarely on flat surfaces,' supporting the speed-dependent sensory feedback hypothesis.

result: In flies, interleg coordination is not dominated by sensory feedback; instead, communication between CPGs, perhaps by local interneurons, may be sufficient for coordination, and when all legs are equally impaired, flies resort to a CPG and interneuron-dominated system sufficient to execute tripod gait.
status_reasoning: Reviewers noted 'the surprise here comes because in the well-studied stick insect system, sensory inactivation of a leg disrupts proper interlimb coordination,' implicitly accepting that the fly system differs. They requested contrast with leg amputation studies (Wosnitza et al. 2012) 'as a means of exploring how sensory inputs interact with the locomotory CPGs,' indicating acceptance of the CPG-based coordination mechanism in flies.

result: Coordinated walking requires a complex neural network with CPGs that generate rhythmic motor neuron activity for leg joint flexion/extension, coupled to proprioceptive sensory feedback reporting load and joint position.
status_reasoning: Reviewers expressed concern that 'the Introduction presents a naïve view of how CPGs work and interact with descending inputs and sensory feedback,' requesting that 'the opening paragraph of the manuscript should be reworked to reflect the more sophisticated view of CPGs put forth by the references cited.' This indicates the reviewers found the characterization of CPG function oversimplified or incomplete.

result: In stick insects, sensory feedback from legs in stance phase is required for interleg coordination, as demonstrated by experiments showing that stimulation of sensory afferents in the midleg is required for mid and foreleg steps to be out of phase.
status_reasoning: Reviewers used stick insect findings as the established baseline for comparison, stating 'the surprise here comes because in the well-studied stick insect system, sensory inactivation of a leg disrupts proper interlimb coordination.' This indicates acceptance of the stick insect literature as valid context for interpreting the fly results.
